newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government promises limit on means-testing.
newsitem.headline: French government promises limit on means-testing.

text.p: France's new leftist government sought on Wednesday to soothe critics of a controversial plan to end generous family allowances for the better-off, saying it had no plans to extend means-testing to other welfare programmes.
"We have no intention to extend this to other sectors of the social protection system," government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said after a cabinet meeting.
"This is a measure that specifically affects family allowances," she told reporters.

The Socialist-led government, facing a first test of its resolve, has come under fierce criticism from trade unions, family associations and its Communist allies after announcing that households earning more than 25,000 francs ($4,400) a month with two children would no longer receive the 667 franc ($117) monthly allowance.

Critics fear the move could be a cautious first step towards making France's costly and largely indiscriminate welfare state more selective to focus increasingly limited resources on those most in need.
Employment Minister Martine Aubry had insisted on Tuesday that the three-week-old government was open to discussions but would not back down on the principle of shifting resources to the poor.

"This country will have to accept we are in a crisis, that there are children...who cannot get health care, who cannot go on holiday, who cannot get access to culture, who cannot afford lunch in the school canteen," she told parliament.
She said the measure would affect fewer than 10 percent of the 4.1 million families which receive the benefit.
Marc Blondel, leader of the Force Ouvriere labour union, said unions generally opposed capping benefits because it could set a precedent for social security and health insurance.
But analysts said the family allowance was far from the first social benefit to be subject to means-testing.
Others with income ceilings include rental subsidies, aid to single parents and child-care benefits.
"There is nothing revolutionary in this proposal," said one analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

"There are arguments for this and there are arguments against, but there are many programmes with ceilings, and that particular branch of the social security fund is running a deficit," the analyst said.
"Fully half of social services are conditioned on one's resources," said Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande.
"I think it's a lobby," he said. "It is not defending all families but just five to 10 percent of families," he told Radio Luxembourg.
"I think the French people see the need to reserve the family allowances for the really needy," he said.
